newsitem.title: UK: Can "anorak" darling Gateway woo the mainstream?.
newsitem.headline: Can "anorak" darling Gateway woo the mainstream?.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Upstart computer manufacturer Gateway 2000 Inc has generated big sales in Europe wooing computerphiles by mail order, but analysts wonder if the success rate can be maintained with mainstream buyers.
Last year the North Sioux City, South Dakota based Gateway raised its sales by just over 40 percent in Europe to 250,000, according to computer market researcher CONTEXT.
And this was despite a depressed market in Europe, according to a report today from International Data Corp of the U.S.
About 90 percent of Gateway sales are desk-top Personal Computers (PCs), with the remainder portables.

Gateway has so far concentrated on selling to the PC literate by advertising in computer magazines and filling orders by mail. It carries very little inventory, and says that this method of selling allows it to offer the lowest prices, and be the fastest competitor to bring new technology to consumers.
CONTEXT analyst Emmanuel Lalloz said Gateway has been undeniably successful in this niche of the market. The test will come when this is saturated, and computerphobes must be courted.
In an interview, Robert Cheng, Gateway's managing director for Europe, said the "nerd" market is far from saturated.

1996 was the year of price cuts; 1997 will be the year when customers are wowed by technical developments like Intel Corp's new MMX chip technology, which will allow video and audio to be successfully transmitted to PCs, Cheng said.
The spectacular acceleration in Gateway's sales will go on.

"We call our customers "enthusiasts" - people who love their PCs and like to watch the technology move. In 1997 this will move a lot. 1996 was a year of cost cuts but there was not a lot of technological change in the market," Cheng said.
Gateway serves five markets in Europe-U.K., France, Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands-from its Dublin factory.
Its market share of between three and four percent puts it just behind the likes of Siemens AG of Germany and Italy's Olivetti, but way down from market leader COMPAQ's around 13 percent.
Gateway says it will continue to make inroads in the market.
"1997 will be very good for Gateway worldwide and in Europe. We expect to grow at twice the rate of any market we are in."
Cheng said each PC Gateway sells is custom built.

"All PCs are used slightly differently so we tailor exactly to their needs. We only carry parts inventory to build the computers; we don't have a pipeline to a retail store or an inventory in a store."

"So when technology changes or when costs drop very quickly we can pass that on to the customer faster. Our products are always one generation ahead in cost or technology advantage. They get the latest products for the best cost."
Cheng concedes that sales in a mass market call for a different plan, but says this has already started in the U.S.
CONTEXT's Lalloz is confident Gateway can make the transition. It will be boosted by its perception in the market.

"Gateway is recognised by consumers as providing solid machines which work well with good technology. Look at the (magazine) reviews-they come out ahead in all of them. I think they'll go next for the SOHO (small office, home office) market and penetrate that," Lalloz said.
"But first they have a lot to do. They must expand geographically to make sure they are everywhere in Europe."
